title: Ambedkar refuses the book
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: a copy of the Manusmriti on a fire, lit on purpose, in public
carry: untouchability is abolished, and the book refused
tomorrow: Manu lists four roots of dharma. what's the surprising last one?

lines: A BOOK ON A FIRE, IN PUBLIC.
cards: Sometimes the honest answer to something that hurt people isn't a better reading of it. It's no. B.
R. Ambedkar, a lawyer and scholar born into a community treated as untouchable, didn't write a gentler commentary on the Manusmriti. He set a copy on fire, in public, on purpose.
It wasn't a stunt. It was a statement made where everyone could see it.

teach.b: Ambedkar read the dharma books closely, and he read them from where their ranking pushed people: the bottom. The Manusmriti ranks people by birth, and it sets hard limits on those it places low, and on women.
He saw that ranking still shaping ordinary life: who could draw water from which well, who could walk into which temple. So he didn't argue for a kinder reading.
He rejected the book, and the fire said so. He went further.
He helped version India's Constitution, and it says plainly that untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. Here's why this belongs in a lesson on Hindu tradition.
A tradition is more than its books. It's also the people who argue with them, and sometimes the people who refuse them.

teach.h: A RANGE OF VIEWS, ALL IN THE STORY.
teach.b: Hindus today hold a range of views on the Manusmriti. Some read it as history, the record of one age. Some keep a few household rites from it and set the rest down.

Some reject it outright, as Ambedkar did. This week has now seen three ways: Vidyasagar reasoning inside the books, a handful of rice kept, and a fire. Each is part of the story of what was kept, and what was let go.

how: Hindus today hold a range of views on the Manusmriti: some read it as history, some keep a few household rites from it, and some reject it outright, as Ambedkar did.

games.q: your school's founding charter has a rule that once kept some students out. a classmate says: defend all of it, or you're not loyal. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: a community includes the people who argue with its founding texts.
defend every line, or leave the school.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or look at the nearest tap or bottle. Rest your eyes on it for the whole sit, and let yourself remember that for some people, where they could draw water was decided by birth.
When the bell comes, drink slowly, if you like.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected, sometimes out loud: Ambedkar's fire, and a constitution that abolished untouchability.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi asprishyata, untouchability: the practice the Constitution abolished.

carryVoice: For the road: untouchability is abolished, and the book that ranked people by birth was refused out loud. That's part of the story too. Back tomorrow.
